synthesis.body: When two checking surfaces claim parity over the same shape — e.g. `lint-agents-md.py` accepting both real symlinks and a one-line file containing `"AGENTS.md"` for the repo-root CLAUDE.md alias, and `self_host.py`'s drift detector being asked to match — the natural Python idioms `bytes.strip()` and `str.strip()` differ in what counts as whitespace. `bytes.strip()` only strips ASCII whitespace (`\t \n \r \v \f` + space); `str.strip()` strips Unicode whitespace too (NBSP U+00A0, IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, etc.). A `CLAUDE.md` containing `"\xc2\xa0AGENTS.md\xc2\xa0"` (NBSP-padded) passes a `read_text(...).strip() == "AGENTS.md"` lint but fails a `disk_bytes.strip() == b"AGENTS.md"` gate. The realistic window is narrow (no Windows checkout produces NBSP padding) but the docstring/spec claim 'mirrors check #2's strip() semantics' becomes a lie unless the gate decodes first: `disk_bytes.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").strip() == "AGENTS.md"`. Surfaced in round-2 adversarial review of AC15b (PR #77). General rule: when two surfaces claim parity, test both the acceptance side AND the rejection-boundary side, and pick predicates from the same domain (both bytes or both str) — not the convenient mix.

title: Cross-surface parity (lint vs drift gate): `bytes.strip()` and `str.strip()` are not equivalent — Unicode whitespace creates a silent acceptance gap
